citation.title: Deep reinforcement learning for engineering design through topology optimization of elementally discretized design domains
citation.authors: Nathan (K.) Brown, Anthony P. Garland, Georges M. Fadel, Gang Li
citation.venue: Materials & Design, Vol. 218, article 110672 (gold OA, CC-BY, per OpenAlex)
citation.version_coded: Could not render the Materials & Design version of record itself: doi.org/10.1016/j.matdes.2022.110672 and the queue-listed https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0264127522002933/pdf both return only an empty client-side-rendered ScienceDirect app shell to a plain HTTP fetch (no article text in the HTML), and a direct WebFetch of the same URLs returns HTTP 403; OpenAlex nonetheless marks the article is_oa=true/oa_status=gold/license=CC-BY. Checked OpenAlex's two OSTI (US DOE) location records for this DOI (osti.gov/biblio/1867970 and /1872010, both citing this exact DOI/journal/volume, Research Org = Sandia National Laboratories, Sponsoring Org = DOE/NNSA) and the OSTI public API: neither exposes a full-text PDF for the journal DOI itself. A web search surfaced a separate, directly downloadable OSTI PDF, osti.gov/servlets/purl/1898470 (report no. SAND2021-14482C, an AAAI-copyrighted conference-formatted paper by the same four authors, same title, same Clemson/Sandia affiliations). Its abstract, methods, reward function, RL architecture, training procedure (5000 episodes, ~1.5 h, Intel Core i7-10510U CPU), progressive-refinement scheme (6x6 to 12x12 to 24x24) and gradient-based-solver comparison table are a complete, self-contained account of the same study; this appears to be the AAAI symposium/workshop precursor to the Materials & Design journal article rather than the final typeset journal text, and it may omit content the journal version added. This is the version actually read and coded below; DOAJ's location for this DOI (doaj.org/article/3b5c48ea6a4f48e6a5061d80473c8dba) returned HTTP 403 and was not read.

included.reason: I-QUALITY (full-text determination, on the accessible companion/conference version; this blind second-pass coder has no access to the original title/abstract screening code, and cannot confirm whether the actual journal version adds a quantitative speed comparison)

claim.primary_outcome_paraphrase: Across 6 test load cases (Table 1 / Table C1), a deep-RL agent that sequentially voids elements of a 2D grid to minimize strain energy under a volume-fraction target produces 24x24 topologies whose final strain energy is lower than a traditional gradient-based TO solver's (Sigmund's 99-line MATLAB code) in most cases at matched volume fraction, but clearly higher (worse) in one case (1853 vs 929) and at a different, non-matched volume fraction in two others.
claim.key_phrase: achieve reduced strain energies, better satisfying the design objective
claim.location: Results section text plus Table C1, Appendix C (in the accessible AAAI-formatted version); the Abstract and Conclusion state only a qualitative claim ('comparable to a traditional gradient-based topology optimization solver') with no numbers, and no classical-method comparison appears in the Introduction
claim.claimed_speedup_basis: No computation-time or cost comparison against the classical gradient-based solver appears anywhere in the accessible text; the only timing figure given is the RL agent's own training time (5000 episodes, about 1.5 hours on an Intel Core i7-10510U CPU), with no classical-solver time stated to pair it against. The Abstract's 'computational efficiency' phrase refers to RL versus other ML paradigms, not versus the classical solver.
claim.alternatives: Per-case detail from Table C1 (RL strain energy/volume fraction vs gradient-based solver's): (A) 864/0.25 vs 964/0.25 - RL better at matched VF; (B) 193/0.25 vs 211/0.25 - RL better at matched VF; (C) 629/0.31 vs 806/0.25 - RL used more material (VF 0.31 vs 0.25), so not a matched comparison despite lower SE; (D) 1853/0.25 vs 929/0.25 - RL clearly worse (about double the strain energy) at matched VF; (E) 879/0.25 vs 1000/0.25 - RL better at matched VF; (F) 1021/0.16 vs 1245/0.2 - RL used less material and had lower SE, but VF is not matched. The Abstract/Conclusion's qualitative 'comparable to a traditional gradient-based...solver' framing is a secondary candidate outcome if the reader takes the qualitative statement over the table.

baseline.classical_method: Gradient-based topology optimization (compliance/strain-energy minimization under a volume-fraction constraint), using Sigmund's 99-line MATLAB SIMP code (Sigmund 2001, cited directly) as the comparator
baseline.implementation: Sigmund's published 99-line MATLAB implementation (an openly published educational/reference code, not further modified or optimized as described in this version)
baseline.solver: not stated (the 99-line code's default linear solver, typically MATLAB's built-in sparse direct backslash, is not named in this text)
baseline.hardware_ml: Intel Core i7-10510U CPU @ 1.80 GHz, 16 GB RAM, used for RL training (no GPU mentioned)
baseline.problem_size: 2D grids up to 24x24 elements (progressively refined from 6x6 through 12x12 to 24x24)
baseline.ml_time: RL training: 5000 episodes, about 1.5 hours (stated once, for training only; no inference/deployment time per topology is given)
baseline.training_time: 5000 episodes, about 1.5 hours, on the CPU above; training performed only at the coarse 6x6 resolution to limit FEA cost per step
baseline.data_generation_cost: not applicable as a separate cost: training data come from the agent's own online interaction (randomly generated load cases) with the RL environment during the 5000-episode training run, not a pre-generated dataset
baseline.quality_metric: Strain energy (SE, the compliance-equivalent objective) and volume fraction (VF) of the final proposed topology, with SE computed by a 2D plane-stress finite element analysis (FEA) solver used throughout (both to build the RL observation's stress layer and, implicitly, to score the final designs in Table C1)
baseline.quality_gap: See claim.alternatives for the full per-case numbers; net picture across the 6 cases is mixed (3 clear RL wins at matched VF, 1 clear RL loss at matched VF, 2 cases where VF itself differs between methods)

R1.evidence: Table C1 reports strain energy and volume fraction for both methods on the same 6 load cases, computed via the same FEA-based objective, so the comparison metric itself is consistent. But the match is loose: volume fraction differs between the two methods in 2 of 6 cases (C: 0.31 vs 0.25; F: 0.16 vs 0.2), so those two comparisons are not at equal design constraint; and in case (D) the RL topology has roughly double the strain energy of the gradient-based solver's, which sits uneasily with the table caption's claim that the RL agent 'can achieve reduced strain energies' - the caption overstates what the table itself shows for that case.

R2.evidence: No speed or cost claim against the classical solver is made in the accessible text, so efficiency criteria (a)-(e) do not bear on this outcome. For the record: the classical comparator is Sigmund's 99-line MATLAB code, an openly published educational implementation - exactly the kind of implementation the protocol's own R2 partial criterion names ('an unvectorized educational code') - though this cannot be scored since no timing claim is made to test it against.

R3.evidence: No speed or cost claim against the classical method is made anywhere in the accessible text. For the record, training cost is reported on its own (5000 episodes, ~1.5 hours, stated CPU), but it is never paired with a classical-solver time to form an efficiency claim.

R4.evidence: Strain energy is computed via an actual 2D FEA solver on the returned topology (not an image-similarity metric), and volume fraction is reported for every shown case (Table 1/C1), satisfying the core quality-verification requirement. However, 'illegal' actions (disconnected/hinge-point, non-singular-body topologies) are prevented architecturally during the RL rollout rather than measured; no failure or infeasibility rate is reported for the design process, and it is not stated how many attempted test cases (if any) failed to reach a usable design before the 6 shown results were obtained.

reporting.n_test_cases: 6 test load cases (Table 1 / Table C1), each shown at three progressive-refinement resolutions (6x6, 12x12, 24x24); 2 of the 6 use multiple loaded elements, a configuration not seen during training

notes: Access note: the actual Materials & Design (ScienceDirect) rendering of this article could not be obtained despite being marked gold/CC-BY open access by OpenAlex - every URL tried (DOI redirect, ScienceDirect landing page, ScienceDirect /pdf path, two OSTI biblio pages for the same DOI, the OSTI public API, DOE PAGES, DOAJ) either returned an empty JavaScript-only page shell, an HTTP 403, or had no attached full text. The document actually read and coded (osti.gov/servlets/purl/1898470, SAND2021-14482C) is, to the best I can determine, the AAAI conference/symposium version of the same study by the same four authors, matching on title, authors, method, and specific figures (5000 training episodes, ~1.5 hours, 6x6-to-24x24 progressive refinement) independently surfaced by a web search of the target ScienceDirect page. Its content appears complete and self-contained (full methods, a dedicated results table comparing RL to a gradient-based solver, appendices, references), but it may differ from the final Materials & Design typeset text in ways I cannot verify (e.g., additional test cases, an added speed/cost comparison, revised numbers) - the stratum/rule verdicts above reflect only what is present in this accessible version, and stratum='quality' could change if the published journal version adds an explicit speed comparison that this earlier version lacks. Screening-code caveat: as a blind second-pass coder I have no access to the original title/abstract screening file, so 'I-QUALITY' reflects only this full-text read. No author of this article is named Jun Wang (authors: Nathan Brown, Anthony P. Garland, Georges M. Fadel, Gang Li).
